en: The Sūtra on Prince Guṇaprabha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly.
The Buddha was accompanied by a multitude of one thousand two hundred and fifty [monks] and five hundred bodhisattvas.

At that time, the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla was staying in the city of Śrāvastī for the three months of the summer retreat; having newly prepared his robes and bowl and donned his vestments, he was together with a hundred newly ordained bhikṣus.
Having completed what was to be done, they traveled together through various kingdoms until they reached the city of Rājagṛha and Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Thereupon, the venerable Rāḍhāgupta proceeded to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Ratthapāla asked the World-Honored One:
"What does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice so as to attain all extraordinary dharmas of merit, to achieve unshakable and fearless wisdom and transcendent insight;
to manifest eloquence, with radiance that shines through all, entering into omniscience and instructing sentient beings?"
How can they attain liberation and sever all doubt; how, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), can they manifest all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*);
how can their words and deeds correspond; how can they, when questioning the Buddhas, always attain the Buddhas' intent through skillful means;
and how can they receive, uphold, and swiftly realize all-knowledge regarding every Dharma they hear?
At that time, the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, having offered praise with verses and addressed the Buddha, spoke in verse, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva fulfill their practice?"
What is meant by "acting with thorough discernment"?
One who is fully endowed with wisdom, merit, and vows—now the Honored One among Men explains this:
his wondrous body is the color of purple-polished gold; as the Honored One among Men, he has accumulated supreme virtues.
Rescuing and protecting all sentient beings, may the Buddha explain the supreme practice:
how one attains inexhaustible wisdom and the unsurpassed path of immeasurable dhāraṇīs.
How does one attain impartial conduct?
By resolving the doubts of all people; though they delight in birth and death for countless billions of kalpas, their minds never harbor revulsion or weariness.
Having seen countless beings undergoing toil and suffering, he skillfully employs expedient means to instruct them and bring them to understanding;
he purifies his buddha-field and its retinue, and likewise his radiance, lifespan, and assembly.

All that is spoken is but silence; we only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the supreme practice—subduing the hosts of Māra, severing all views, liberating from craving and desire, and transcending perception and mental formations.
How does one expound the meaning of the sutras and dharmas?
We pray that the Buddha will explain the practices of the true practitioners;
with upright and exquisite eloquence, speak with gentle tones for the sake of the multitude.
Satisfying the world like a timely rain, may the Buddha explain all the practices of awakening.
Your speech is as subtle as the *kacchāpī* lute, a Brahma-voice with the sound of certain and clear wisdom.
As the assembly thirsts for and yearns for the Dharma of the sutras, you satisfy them all with the nectar of immortality.
If there are those who wish to study the sublime path of the Buddha, they should be diligent and energetic, setting their will upon the practice of the Dharma.
All that the Tathāgata has taught is entirely equal; we only pray that the King of Dharma will speak it at this time.
I wish to hear the teaching of the True and Right Path; the Buddha, the God among Gods, knows my intent.
Now I do not dare to disturb the World-Honored One; I only pray that you will well expound the Unsurpassed Practice.
The Buddha said to Rāṣṭrapāla:
"Excellent, excellent!
That you should ask the Tathāgata about such a meaning."

With great compassion and a desire for the peace and security of many, he takes pity on the devas and the people of the world, and thus provides for the future bodhisattvas, enabling them to attain the protection of their practice.
Ratthapāla! Listen attentively and reflect upon this well!
"I shall explain it for you. Rāṣṭrapāla replied,
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said, "Rāṣṭrapāla!"
Bodhisattvas have four dharmas by which they attain pure conduct. What are these four?
First, they practice a mind of equanimity, free from flattery and deceit.
Second, to maintain an impartial mind toward all beings;
third, to understand and realize the practice of emptiness;
fourth, for one's physical conduct to accord with what one speaks.
"These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva swiftly attains pure conduct.
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains peaceful encouragement and progress."
What are the four?
First, attaining dhāraṇī;
second, attaining virtuous friends;
Third, attaining the patience of the Dharma;
fourth, being pure in precepts and practicing with equanimity—
these are the four dharmas.
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
"A bodhisattva further possesses four dharmas by which they enter into the realm of afflictions and encourage others in the dharmas of birth and death.
What are these four?"
First, the Bodhisattva manifests the body of a Buddha and enters into birth and death to exhort those subject to arising and ceasing, causing them to attain the Dharma of joy;
second, he preaches the Dharma of pliancy and compliance;
third, he possesses nothing that he does not give away without attachment.
"Fourth, attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas;
these are the four dharmas.
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
“Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva is free from attachment.
What are these four?
First, a bodhisattva should not be attached to a home or a dwelling.”
Second, an ordained bodhisattva should not covet wealth or profit;
third, a bodhisattva should not seek the retribution of various merits;
fourth, a bodhisattva should not cherish their own body or life.
"These are the four dharmas.
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva never tires of the Dharma."
What are the four?
First, to have no deficiency or diminution in one's precepts;
second, to practice dwelling in seclusion in the wilderness.
Third, to practice the conduct of the four noble ones;
fourth, to attain extensive learning.
These are the four dharmas.
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
“There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains non-conceptualization and universal entry. What are the four?
First, causing them to be born in favorable realms and always encounter the era of a Buddha;
second, listening to and receiving the instructions of elders and superiors without flattery or deceit;
third, delighting in receiving commands and instructions, with a mind that does not cling to wealth or profit.
"Fourth, one attains eloquence to enter into the essential points of the profound Dharma;
these are the four dharmas.
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
“A bodhisattva has four dharmas by which they attain pure conduct. What are these four?
First, practicing the bodhisattva path, one harbors no intent to harm others.”
Second, to cast aside flattery, sycophancy, and the conduct of the heterodox and false, and to delight in dwelling in seclusion;
third, to give away all that one possesses without stinginess and without seeking recompense;
fourth, to constantly set one's mind on seeking the Dharma day and night, and upon seeing those who preach the Dharma, not to seek out their faults.
"These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains pure conduct.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"When the mind does not cling to dusty and defiled dharmas, Then there will be no evil flaws or impurities."
With a resolute mind that never tires of teaching and discussing the Dharma, one can bring about the attainment of the unsurpassed path.
Even when encountering those who are not virtuous, one always maintains a single-minded focus;

universally entering into the roots of deviant conduct and evil paths, one leaves the household life to study the Way without any sense of loss, dwelling among the mountains with the desire for liberation.
Dwelling in seclusion in solitude, nothing arises within; his mind does not cling to wealth, profit, or form.
He casts aside his body and cherishes not his life; his conduct is like that of a lion, free from fear.
His heart attains joy and knows contentment, just as a soaring bird has nothing to dread.
All worlds are devoid of permanence; with great wisdom, one aspires to the path of the Buddha.
Always delighting in solitude like a rhinoceros, one is fearless like a lion;
the mind is without terror or anxiety, and there is no coarse intent. Whether receiving offerings or not, one neither increases nor diminishes.
Having cast aside perverse speech and evil views, with wisdom one understands the great practice and resolves upon the Way;
I am the protector of all in the world, my mind employing skillful means without negligence.
With a mind that skillfully upholds the precepts, one becomes a guide for the multitude;

with a heart free from the distraction of various attachments and cravings, one reverently follows right conduct as if extinguishing a fire, constantly seeking the supreme and wondrous practice of the World-Honored One.
Already liberated from emptiness and non-conceptualization, fully endowed with all qualities, he discerns profound stillness;
dwelling in tranquility with luminous wisdom, he attains the taste of the nectar of immortality and is ever joyful.
Even if one attains the Buddha’s mind of awakening, one should always remain pure and free from doubt;
with total retention and eloquence, unify the mind, and endure all suffering without seeking recompense.
If there are bodhisattvas who hear of these practices, And wish to seek the Buddha-way, they should rejoice;
Always intent on diligence and free from indolence, They understand defilement and ignorance, their minds free from harm.
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva falls away from his state.
What are these four?"
First, a bodhisattva who is arrogant and lacks reverence brings about their own downfall;
second, a bodhisattva who acts without gratitude and practices flattery brings about their own downfall;
third, a bodhisattva who seeks offerings and craves profit brings about their own downfall.
Fourth, when a bodhisattva employs flattery, deceit, and evil conduct in seeking offerings, they bring about their own downfall;
these are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva brings about their own downfall.
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva falls into the trench of error.
What are these four?"
First, laziness is a dharma that leads to falling into a pit;
second, a lack of pure faith;
third, the arising of conceptualizations.
"Fourth, seeing those who receive offerings, one harbors a mind of jealousy;
these are the four things by which a bodhisattva falls into the ditches of deviance.
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
“A bodhisattva should not practice four types of things. What are these four?
First, a bodhisattva should not associate with those who hold false views.”
Second, a bodhisattva should not associate with those who slander the true Dharma;
third, a bodhisattva should not associate with evil associates;
fourth, a bodhisattva should not associate with those who are greedy for food and clothing.
"These are the four dharmas.
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva incurs the retribution of suffering."
What are the four?
First, to be conceited on account of one's wisdom and to harbor a mind of malice and envy;
second, to have no joy in the heart and no pure conduct.
Third, being unable to practice forbearance and desiring only to covet the wealth and property of others;
fourth, maintaining the notion of a self or person and becoming attached to dharmas.
These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva incurs the sin of suffering.
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
“Furthermore, there are four things by which a bodhisattva binds himself.
What are these four?
First, when a bodhisattva delights in treating others with contempt, this is self-binding;
second, when a bodhisattva engages in worldly crafts and gives rise to thoughts of trade and livelihood, this is self-binding;
third, when a bodhisattva’s mind does not accept the wisdom of the Dharma and acts with negligence, this is self-binding.
"Fourth, when a bodhisattva’s bound mind dwells within the lineage, this constitutes self-bondage;
these are the four matters.
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
"In future ages, there will be those who study the bodhisattva path and yet possess such defilements and fail to practice.
They will honor those who lack practice—those who are sycophantic; they will honor those who are sycophantic—those who are ignorant; and they will honor those who are ignorant:

those who greedily seek clothing and food, who lack an upright mind, who envy noble lineages, who are sycophantic and harbor depravity, who lack a simple and honest heart, and who deceive their elders and their own families for the sake of receiving offerings."

They instead slander one another; their minds are greedy for wealth and profit as they travel through various commanderies and kingdoms. They do not contemplate preaching the Dharma to enlighten and liberate others, nor do they possess skillful means (*upāya*).
Lacking wisdom toward the multitude, they consider themselves wise;
yet when they see others who possess wisdom and are virtuous teachers, they treat them with contempt.
Those who possess no practice are vessels of destruction.
Seeking out one another’s faults and abandoning the practice of vigor, they are ignorant and indolent; they do not cultivate much wisdom and instead ruin the Dharma among themselves.

They cause the assembly to be divided and create mutual enmity and harm, turning to quarrel with one another while claiming, "The others have no practice, whereas I uphold the teachings of the Dharma."
Not upholding the prohibitions and precepts, having no desire to hear the Dharma, and failing to practice diligence, they are born into poverty and destitution within households of misery.
Acting as śramaṇas, they worry only about seeking wealth and profit; they cannot find peace even in their own dwellings, let alone when their minds are distracted.
"Though they practice the Buddha’s merits with a single mind, they continue to crave the benefits of family life, yet claim of themselves, 'I am a śramaṇa.
The Buddha said:

'I do not say that such people as these are practicing the Dharma of a bodhisattva. For hundreds of thousands of kalpas, such persons cannot even attain the patient acceptance of accordance with the Dharma (anulomikī kṣānti), let alone desire to attain the practice of the Buddha's wisdom and perfect enlightenment."
The Buddha said, “Rāṣṭrapāla!
I do not say only that such people fall into the moat of the three paths; they shall also fall into the eight states of woe.”
What are the eight?
First, being born in a remote region;
second, falling into a poor family.
Third, one will have an ugly and hideous countenance in whatever place one is born;
fourth, one will be born into a family that is perverse and evil, opposed to goodness;
fifth, one will be born to associate with evil companions.
Sixth, they will suffer from many illnesses;
seventh, their lifespan will be short in whatever place they are born;
eighth, they will die an untimely death.
These are the eight evil matters for a bodhisattva that cause one to fall into the trench of heterodoxy.
Why is this so? Rāṣṭrapāla!

I do not consider making vows with mere words to be the practice of a bodhisattva; I do not regard those who are hypocritical and disorderly as possessing pure conduct; I do not take flattery and deceit to be the practice of a bodhisattva; I do not consider attachment to food and clothing to be making offerings to the Buddha; I do not call those who are arrogant ones of pure wisdom; and I do not take the practice of one's own views as a means to sever the defilement of doubt.

I do not say that one who is envious possesses a pure mind; I do not say that one who is full of craving attains dhāraṇī; I do not say that one who does not perceive the virtue of the ultimate truth, yet remains obstructed, shall be born in a good realm; and I do not say that one who craves noble lineage and clings to physical beauty shall obtain a pure body.

I do not say that one who practices with conceptualization will attain the concentrated mind of a Buddha; I do not say that one who does not practice with utmost sincerity will attain purity; I do not say that one who is arrogant will attain a pure mind; I do not say that one who does not know contentment will love the Dharma; and I do not say that one who covets body and life is one who aspires to seek the Dharma.
The Buddha said,
"Ratthapāla! I do not harbor resentment or reproach toward the six external teachers."
To rebuke these foolish people is even more severe than [rebuking] the six external teachers. Why is this?
Their words differ from one another and their practices are inconsistent, as they seek to deceive the various devas and the people of the world.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Lacking wisdom and agitated by confusion, they are heedless;
Arrogant, disrespectful, and full of greedy desires, They encounter worldly defilements and give rise to thoughts of lust; Such people as these are far removed from the Way."
Craving offerings increases indolence; through a lack of diligence, one loses pure faith.
Thus, one ruins pure conduct and perishes from right precepts; the violator of the prohibitions loses the path of goodness.
Born into a poor family, he became a śramaṇa; amidst poverty and distress, he sought offerings.
It is like a person who, being destitute and possessing nothing, begs from others in hope of obtaining wealth and property.
Out of greed for offerings, they dwell in seclusion; though residing there, they desire only self-attainment.
Having acquired supernatural powers, wisdom, and eloquence, they abandon their families and take possession of all that exists.
Not seeing the Path, they abide in accordance with distracted conduct;
They are born into poor and lowly families, and amidst the ugly and base, they lack power and influence; They fall into the state of arrogance and folly.
Those who act in a base and lowly manner possess neither fame nor virtue;
with minds greedy for wealth and profit, they become heedless, and subsequently are reborn in great places of suffering, where for billions of eons they leave no trace of goodness.
Even if one were free from greed for gain on the Path, and all gods and humans were to attain Buddhahood,
just as the wind of Sūlana cannot move a person, one does not achieve it for oneself merely through making offerings.
Lacking merit, they look up to others; lacking the intent for diligence, they lose virtuous conduct.
By bringing disorder to the teaching and failing to uphold the Dharma, they cannot attain the aspiration for the path of wisdom.
Through sincerity and benefit, one brings forth the Buddha-dharma; ultimately, one does not lose the practice that accords with the intent of the Way.
One’s vows are exceedingly firm and ever-pure; that which is upheld in accordance with what is appropriate is the Way.
In my quest for the Buddha, I have nothing that I do not cherish; even giving up my body and life, I seek only the Dharma of the sutras.
Yet these people abandon the Dharma and fail to exert themselves, thereby losing the essential meaning of the Path’s teachings.

There is a great lamp-light that none can see; I have originally sought the well-spoken teachings of the True Dharma, and as soon as I heard what was taught, I immediately put it into practice, severing all cravings and desires.
Though one has heard various teachings of the Buddha-dharma, If one cannot master even a single verse, How can one who acts contrary to the Dharma attain the Way?
It would be like showing the path to a blind person.
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
"In the distant past, incalculable kalpas ago—so long, immeasurable, and inconceivable."
At that time, there was a Buddha named Kṣemadatta Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Teacher in the World, Buddha, God among Gods.
"At that time, there was a king named Aṭṭhanna.
The Buddha said, "Rāṣṭrapāla!"
The King of Aṭaṇḍu reigned over Jambudvīpa, which was sixty-four thousand li in breadth and length.
At that time, Jambudvīpa contained twenty thousand great cities and one billion households.

The King Aṭaṇḍu had a great city named Ratnaprabhāsa, which was his seat of governance. That city was four hundred and eighty li in length and two hundred and eighty li in breadth; it was constructed of the seven treasures, with eight roads leading out toward the south and north, all of which were meticulously crafted and complete in every detail.
At that time, the human lifespan was one billion nayutas of years.
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
"That King Arjuna had a son named Guṇaprabha, who was exceptionally handsome and of peerless majesty."
At the moment of his initial birth, a thousand treasuries spontaneously emerged, all composed of the seven precious gems;
within each treasury, there were naturally the treasures of various kings, these seven jewels being eight zhang in height.
As soon as Guṇaprabha was born, all the people of Jambudvīpa were filled with great joy; those confined in prisons and dungeons were all set free.
Within seven days of his birth, there was no wisdom he did not master, and he was fully endowed with both worldly and spiritual knowledge.
The Buddha said to Rāṣṭrapāla:
"At that time, during the middle watch of the night, the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens came to the place where Prince Puṇyaraśmi was and said to him: 'Prince!'"
"One should not engage in heedless conduct.
Thereupon, from that time forward throughout ten thousand years, Prince Guṇaprabha never slept nor engaged in playful diversion;
he never danced or sang, nor did he ever perform music.
They neither come nor go, nor do they travel about for sightseeing;
they have never craved their own bodies, nor do they think of song, dance, or music;
they do not crave wealth or profit, nor do they think of their homes.
They do not cling to districts or states, nor do they have any desires;
regarding all that exists, they harbor no attachment or stinginess;
they maintain a single-minded concentration, always dwelling in solitary places, thereby pacifying all hardships and attaining a state of few concerns.
"Those who are subject to birth and death cannot preserve their bodies or lives; they do not respect one another, for all those bound by worldly affection must inevitably part.
There is no one to act as a guide, and through violating the Dharma and committing offenses, they are filled with sorrow, anxiety, and fear.
In the realm of ordinary beings, there is no knowledge of contentment; driven by the power of ignorance, they constantly delight in strife and contention."
"I am now fallen into the midst of non-action;
I wish to remain silent and inactive.
At that time, the Prince dwelt alone in seclusion, free from thoughts of negligence, distancing himself from all sensual desires and practicing with equanimity of mind.
The Buddha said to Rāṣṭrapāla:

"At that time, within another realm, King Arjuna had a great city named Dānarata, built for Prince Guṇaprabha. It was eight stories high from south to north and contained eight hundred crossroads; the city was constructed of the seven treasures.
Its sevenfold walls were adorned with curtains made of the seven treasures, all further embellished with necklaces of white pearls."

Between all the railings there were eighty thousand precious pillars; each of these precious pillars was interconnected by sixty thousand precious cords, and each of these precious cords was fastened with one trillion four hundred billion bands.
When the wind blew, they rubbed against one another in succession, producing the sounds of hundreds of thousands of musical instruments.

Before every one of the railings, there were five hundred court ladies who were skilled at playing musical instruments; they were all masters of song and dance, possessing the highest artistic talent and perfecting their craft, capable of delighting the kings and people of all nations throughout the world, and thus providing service to Prince Guṇaprabha.
The King said to his attendants:
"You all must set aside all other affairs and perform various musical performances day and night to delight the Prince, ensuring that he is satisfied and never allowed to see anything unwholesome."

Along all the railings, he placed various articles for giving: food was provided for the hungry, drink for the thirsty, and vehicles and horses were given to those who desired them; furthermore, clothing, flowers, incense, seats, dwellings, and lamps were offered as alms according to whatever each person requested.
He possessed gold, silver, moon-bright pearls, lapis lazuli, crystal, elephants, and horses; with all manner of necklaces made of the seven treasures, he provided for the whole world.
In the center of that city, he constructed for Prince Virtue-Light (*Guangde*) a palace of the seven treasures with eight layers of jeweled lattices;
within that lecture hall, there were four hundred million seats provided for the prince.
Within the city there were gardens and groves where flowering trees and jewel-trees grew; these trees were ever-present and completely covered everything.
The Buddha said to Rāṣṭrapāla:
"In the center of those gardens and groves was a bathing pool made of the seven treasures, with railings fashioned from four precious substances—gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli."
Within it are eight hundred lion heads, through which the water flows into the bathing pool.
Within that bathing pool there are again eight hundred lion heads, from which the pool water flows out.
Within the pond, four kinds of flowers always grow—blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and yellow lotuses;
surrounding it are jewel trees, each of which bears both flowers and fruit.

Along the edges of those bathing pools, there were further eight hundred adorned jewel-trees; between every set of these jewel-trees, there were twelve additional jewel-trees, each interconnected with eighty-eight strands of precious thread.
When the wind arose and blew upon the trees, they struck one another, producing hundreds of thousands of kinds of sounds.
Above each bathing pool was a canopy of interlaced seven-jeweled drapery, within which Prince Virtue-Light bathed.
Above the lecture hall were forty billion couches and seats made of the seven jewels, each spread with five hundred cushions.
In its center was spread a great throne made of the seven treasures, upon which eighty billion exquisite garments were laid out as a seat-cloth;
the throne was five zhang and six chi in height, and Prince De-guang sat upon it.
Beneath every seat there was a censer; three times each day and night, they burned honey-scented incense, scattered various beautiful flowers, covered them with jewels, and hung down golden lotuses.
In the hall there was a canopy of bright moon pearls, from which eighty thousand bright moon pearls hung down, emitting a radiance that illuminated everywhere.
Upon all the trees, various banners and canopies were suspended, and within every garden and pavilion there were ninety thousand bright moon pearls.
The radiance of that single jewel illuminated forty *li*, pervading the entire Buddha-land.
The Buddha said to Rāṣṭrapāla:

“Within that garden pavilion, there were parrots, cormorants, *kukkuṭa* birds, peacocks, geese, mandarin ducks, *kunāla* birds, pheasants, and various *jīvañjīvaka* birds, all of which sang together with diverse melodies to delight Prince Guṇaprabha, who constantly prepared offerings of five hundred flavors.”
"At that time, within all the chambers there were five hundred young men, all between the ages of sixteen and twenty, who had been selected from among all the various kingdoms."
Having obtained these young men, they were led into that city; all were clever and discerning, capable of everything, and fully acquainted with every activity in the world.

Furthermore, eighty billion young women were brought into the city; they were upright and beautiful, aged between sixteen and twenty at most. All were skilled in song and dance, able to delight men. Their speech was gentle and eloquent, always timely—neither too long nor too short. They were neither fat nor thin, neither too fair nor too dark. Their mouths exhaled the fragrance of *utpala* lotuses, and their bodies emitted the scent of sandalwood. Like celestial maidens, they were all of one mind, surrounding Prince Śrīprabha as he played drums and lutes and sang songs.
Thereupon, Prince Virtuous Light thought to himself:
"I have now naturally encountered a great enemy who disturbs my pure and white Dharma; I must now practice deeds for which I have nothing to spare."
Thereupon, the Prince was filled with sorrow and found no joy.
Just as a person who has been captured and imprisoned finds no pleasure in their heart, so it was with Prince Śrīprabha.

Seeing the various court ladies, musicians, and entertainers, his mind was free from indulgence; he did not regard them as extraordinary, nor did he crave their city-walls or become attached to the carriages.

Throughout those thousand years, he remained fully endowed with this practice: he never cherished forms, nor did he even conceive thoughts of them; he eliminated all perceptions of sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile sensations.

Constantly focused with a single-minded resolve, he thought: "These are the hosts of my enemies. How can I carry myself out from among these enemies so as to attain liberation and practice without negligence?"
At that time, the female attendants said to King Aṭṭhaka:
"The prince does not permit singing and dancing; he is sorrowful and finds no joy.
The Buddha said to Rāṣṭrapāla:

At that time, King Aṅgīrasa, together with eighty thousand minor kings, went to the place where Prince Guṇaprabha was; weeping with tears streaming down, filled with grief and sorrow, he fell to the ground in a faint.
The attendants immediately supported him together, and the King had him stand up and spoke these verses for the sake of the Prince:
“May you, my son, first behold my various treasures, which appeared spontaneously at the time of your birth.
Tell me now who has provoked you; I shall punish that offender with severe penalties.”
Now let us look upon this as if it were heaven; according to your wishes, O son, whatever the Prince now lacks, I can provide for you to obtain it at will.
Beholding these various desires with pure and beautiful eyes, amidst the sounds of drums and music played by all the court ladies, he enjoys their company to dispel his sorrow;
they are all skilled in the art of drumming and always laugh with joy.
You should listen to these exquisite sounds, as the struck musical instruments blend in mournful harmony;
now is the very time for the mind’s enjoyment, for within the waters of this pond there are lotus flowers.
Within the garden groves are flowers, leaves, and fruits, Of every kind, wondrous and fine, without disorder or impurity;
This vision is the foremost wisdom of mastery— May you take joy in it and have compassion for me alone.
Entering the pond, they sprinkle water and enjoy themselves at will;
within it are lotuses of blue, yellow, and white, and various red flowers whose radiance awakens the mind. Why is it that you, my son, look upon this and find no joy?
Cormorants, parrots, *kukkuṭa* cranes, and *koṇāgaka* birds with the mournful cries of pheasants;
various fragrant white flowers like snow—who, upon hearing these sounds, would not be filled with joy?
The Bright Moon Lecture Hall possesses the power of equality; its railings are made of gold and lapis lazuli.
All manner of rare jewels are most exquisite and beautiful, and from the various trees issue sounds numbering in the hundreds of koṭis.

Because I have bestowed these upon you by the side of the balustrade, you hear the sounds of drums and flutes from thousands of court ladies, as well as the songs and music of celestial maidens; why, my son, do you not feel joy in your heart?
Now that you, Prince and others, are so beautiful and handsome, you may enjoy yourselves; listen to my words.
Your parents dwell here with tears falling from their eyes; do you have no compassion for us?
At that time, Prince Guṇaprabha replied to the king in verse:
“That possessor of merit speaks words free from all evil views;
I, weary of suffering and pleasure, have no craving for gain or desire.”
I see all the people of the five realms of birth and death;
now I shall speak of liberation—O Father King, listen to my words.
Since no one can disturb me, what more should I say now?
I have no craving for sensual desires; how could I delight in song and dance?
All forms of love and desire I regard as enemies.
The various cravings of worldly toil follow people into the five realms of existence.
These various female attendants take no pleasure in the delusion of awakening;
they are the works of Māra, which bind people according to their inclinations.
The noble sages and practitioners of the Way never praise them.
Those who habituate themselves to these sensual desires sow the roots of causal conditions;
this body of a courtesan is like leather bound together,
with tendons and bones propping each other up— a mere illusion, devoid of true benefit.
It is like a painted jar, filled to the brim with impurities;
it is like being amidst a cemetery—how could one find delight in this?
As for the sounds of music played, they have no existence and no recipient.
All pleasures lack true reality; to understand this is to be free from delusion.
If one habituates oneself to conceptual thoughts, one immediately loses single-minded concentration.
One who follows the sounds of worldly toil is like a foolish old man.
Of all the trees of existence, some may flourish intensely, yet they cannot be found forever; some may be devoid of joy.
Their fruit is not constant, nor do they ever remain permanently attached to the tree.
Since I have realized this, how could I ever play with my short life?
One cannot rely upon one's parents, nor upon brothers or a wife;
it is the same for kinsmen—for at the moment of death, there is no autonomy.
All that exists is like dew upon the grass;
one should not allow the mind to run wild, indulging in self-will and negligence.
This mind can never be satisfied, for it is like the great ocean.
Affection is exceedingly vast; having already attained it, one seeks it again.
Because all people are driven by craving and desire, each becomes indolent and negligent;
yet there is none who can diminish it, just like Mount Sumeru.
Human beings take the mind as their foundation;
body and life pass away with rapidity, like the flow of a river, meeting only to part again.
They perish utterly and do not endure for long, being just like a flash of lightning.
To be greedily attached to the desires of the three realms is to lack wisdom.
The devas have come to tell me: "Do not be negligent;
as one who practices the path of a bodhisattva, do not crave any possessions."
One who wishes to attain the Buddha-way and compassionately regards all people cannot reach the Buddha-way through the practice of lustful desire.
Those who embrace greed and become slaves to their own minds [cannot do so either].
Thus one brings about one's own ruin and cannot establish meritorious virtue.
I shall never accept sensual desires, nor shall I give rise to anger;
like a bird fallen into a net, how could one attain mastery?
When evil thoughts manifest, they bind one’s own body;
the mind loses its sovereignty and becomes a heap of misfortune.
Craving is a body of fear, like the blossoms of a poisonous tree.
Who is this person worthy of honor? It is he who has crossed over the swift waters;
who beholds all people falling into the evil realms.
For the sake of disputing empty and non-existent propositions, they give rise to various false views.
O King, you should know my intention: I wish to deliver and liberate these people.
Without craving for or accumulating arrogant dharmas, they shall swiftly attain the *pāramitā* of deliverance;
I awaken those who are slumbering and heal those afflicted by pestilence.
To eliminate suffering and affliction, and to establish them in the path of joy;
for those who wish to escape the three thousand worlds and are bound by attachment to sounds,
he preaches the meaning of the sublime sutras to satisfy their long-standing poverty.
He disciplines those who have not yet attained realization and pulls them out from the evil realms.
He grants eyes to the blind and enables the deaf to hear;
he creates the lamp of liberation and establishes wisdom and supernormal powers.
Causing all people within the three realms to attain the equality of the three patiences,
he brings down a rain of compassion and delivers them to the far shore beyond clouds and mist.
For the sake of all beings, he manifests the blazing radiance of his light.
He then maintained a virtuous and awakened mind, causing them to be liberated and find cool shade.
He rained down various medicines, ensuring that all attained peace and security;
having thus reflected upon his father, the King, he sat down with single-minded concentration.
Regarding all desires, I no longer have any aspiration or seeking;
I desire only to seek the Buddha-way for the sake of pitying all people.
Regarding the cravings of the various realms of existence, I no longer have any aspiration.
Who among the wise would take pleasure in remaining within this?
Why violate prohibitions, causing the mind to become deluded and confused? If one succumbs to craving for sensual forms, one will fall into the great evil realms.
Whoever practices the Buddha-way should not again succumb to negligence;
while all people follow the flow of the current, I shall now go against it.
It cannot be attained through mere words, yet thus one reaches the Buddha-way.
May you emit the light of compassion and mercy to illuminate all people.
I have no craving for sensual desires, nor am I bound by attachment to wealth and possessions;
I now pray that the Father King will not return with the multitude.
I wish to abandon the great assembly and all the kingdoms;
for many people seek after what is pleasing to their own minds, and from this they bring about illness.
To restrain the mind and not be negligent is superior to gaining a hundred million kingdoms.
One cannot attain the path of Buddhahood while dwelling amidst sensual desires.
If you wish to attain the unsurpassed state of peace and happiness,
you should go into the great mountains and sit beneath a tree.
"By practicing in seclusion, one may attain the noble path of awakening.
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
"At that time, Prince Śrīprabha was in the lecture hall together with those who were indolent; his heart felt revulsion toward them."
At that time, the Prince practiced three modes of conduct. What are these three?
First, standing still;
second, walking in meditation (caṅkrama).
Third, he practiced seated meditation;
casting off sleep and reclining, he fulfilled the higher practices and attained the eighth stage.

At that time, in the middle of the night, the Prince heard a voice in the void, as the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens extolled the Buddha’s merits for being vast, universal, and complete, as well as praising the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
Upon hearing this, Prince Guṇaprabha’s hair stood on end; he immediately shed tears and, distressed and unhappy, joined his palms and addressed the devas with these verses:
“I am in the midst of calamity; O devas, may you have compassion for me!
Please stay for a moment and hear my words, for I wish to ask something.”
"Traveling through the midst of space, for whom do you chant praises?
I hear your voice, and my heart is moved with both sorrow and joy.
The Buddha said to Rāṣṭrapāla:
At that time, the devas spoke these verses for the sake of Prince Virtue-Light:
"In this world there is a Buddha; does the Prince not hear of him?
The Buddha’s name is Kṣema; he provides salvation and offers protection.
He practices all roots of goodness and manifests the honored merit of transformation.
The assembly of monks, through their learning, numbers in the thousands of billions.
Prince Śrīprabha addressed the devas in verse, saying:
"If I were to see the World-Honored One, how would I know that he is a Buddha?"
I pray that you will speak of the merits of loving-kindness, for I wish to know of the Perfectly Awakened One.
Should I go to see the Buddha, what should I ask him?
How does one practice the path of a bodhisattva, so as to become a protector of all beings?
Thereupon, the devas spoke these verses for the sake of Prince Guṇaprabha:
“His hair is soft, wondrous, and beautiful, Exquisite and curling to the right;
The majesty of his uṣṇīṣa-mark Is as lovely as a mountain peak.”
The radiance from the mark between the eyebrows is majestic and brilliant like the rising sun;
it arises wondrously, curling to the right, its color as beautiful and white as snow.
His awakened mind is pure, and his eyes are a deep azure-blue.
The Son of Heaven, Honored Among Men, possesses a countenance of perfect beauty.
His face is always serene and joyful; he emits billions of immeasurable rays of light that pervade the three thousandfold world-system, extinguishing all evil realms.
The teeth within the Buddha’s mouth are all perfectly even and pure;
as fresh and clean as the *kumuda* flower, they possess a brilliance like the light of a fine tree.
Without disorder, there are twenty in each row; together they form these forty.
The tongue within his mouth is exquisite, Reaching back to cover his own face.
The wondrous words spoken from his mouth Cause the hearts of others to rejoice;
Always free from all flattery and deceit, His Brahma-voice is exceedingly pure.
That which the Buddha expounds surpasses a hundred thousand musical performances;
it eliminates all doubts and brings benefit and joy to people.
Lacking none of the various virtues, his skillful means resolve the meaning of the Way.
Having understood the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it becomes a necklace of hundreds of thousands of jewels.
The sounds from that ground become celestial music;
just as the resonance of the heavens, so too is the speech of the Buddha.
The candra-haṃsa, the peacock, the kuṭara and the ruddy goose,
the wild goose, the crane, and the cormorant— Kunāla asked them:
"Is their voice like that of Brahmā, so soft and exceedingly harmonious?"
Without flattery and without deficiency, he has awakened to the meaning of all things.
A preeminent scholar who stands far above others, he satisfies the minds of the wise;
pure and free from slander, he is devoid of all conceptual desires.
He who practices virtue and righteousness well, never hears of his own blemishes;
that practitioner of the Dharma attains perfect awakening, and thus his merits are described.
The body of the World-Honored One is endowed with all manner of colors.
His arms extend below his knees, and his seven parts are all perfectly full;
his fingers are slender and elegant, possessing many exquisite qualities;
his body is the color of purple-polished gold, and his heart is like a bright moon-jewel.
The body hairs are soft and fine, Pointing upward and curling to the right;
They are even and rounded, rising like a mound, And the male organ is retracted and hidden.
The soles of the feet are level and firm, Beneath which are the marks of the wheels.
The Buddha’s knees are most excellent, with various colors in perfect symmetry.
His walking is like that of a dragon king; his gait is like that of a lion.
When he walks, he silently lowers his head, all his faculties utterly pure.
If a person scatters flowers, they transform into a flower canopy;
when there is increase and no decrease, this is the Buddha’s True Dharma.
Whether one gains profit or loss, whether one encounters hardship or ease, [one remains steadfast].
Whether faced with praise and lamentation, or slander and abuse, his mind neither increases nor diminishes.
Like a lotus flower that is not defiled by mud or water,
the True Lion is thus, and there is none equal to him.
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
"At that time, the crown prince Śrīprabha, having heard the praise of the Buddha’s merits as well as those of the Dharma and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus, leaped for joy;
he was like a poor person, suffering from hunger and cold, who discovers a hidden treasure and rejoices."
Just as a blind person who regains their sight,
or a prisoner in a jail who attains liberation, that person rejoices;
so too did the Crown Prince Guṇaprabha rejoice upon hearing the praises of the Buddha’s merits, as well as those of the Dharma and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus.
Thereupon, the Crown Prince Virtuous Light (Guangde) thought to himself:

"Now that I have heard of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, which testifies to the Dharma and the Sangha—complete and with no deficiency in their noble conduct—I see that while remaining within the cycle of birth and death, one must turn back from deviant practices.
Ordinary people for the most part lack gratitude and reciprocity; they are greedy for their own bodies and harbor self-centered views, which is not the right practice."
The household life is full of defilements; those who habitually cling to sensual desires shall fall into suffering.
The heedless practitioner is shunned by the wise, for ignorance is a blinding darkness; therein, one should act as a lamp of equanimity.
The human mind is difficult to tame; name-and-form is profoundly deep; the six sense bases are insatiable, and various habitual tendencies are not severed.
One shall encounter bitter poisons, painful itching, and unrest; with affection as the root, one is bound by shackles and manacles, and the various sensations are difficult to relinquish.
Being joined with existence is to dwell long in enmity; birth and death are difficult to sever, and one is beset by many people and the clamor of manifold affairs.
The body is quickly deluded and disordered, lacking stability, and must inevitably return to death; therein joy is little and sorrow is much. Only the Buddha-dharma is the supreme peace.
One cannot establish meritorious conduct through the practices of worldly affliction or with a mind of greed and negligence.
At present, I am mired in ignorance and cannot attain single-minded concentration.

"One should not, with a mind that delights in birth and death, associate with evil people while merely preparing for the path of goodness; how much less so when one desires to attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path?
I would rather throw myself from a high tower facing east than allow my family and kinsmen to create an obstruction at the gate, preventing me from departing."
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
“At that time, the prince of the king, Guṇaprabha, threw himself toward that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kṣemadharman, speaking these words:
‘If the World-Honored One possesses all-encompassing wisdom that perceives everything universally, then you, O God among Gods, should now think of rescuing me.’”
Thereupon, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śrī-artha extended his right arm and released a radiance from his hand that illuminated Prince Guṇaprabha.

Within that radiance, there appeared spontaneously a thousand-petaled lotus flower as large as a chariot wheel; from that lotus issued hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light, which shone everywhere and penetrated all.

Thereupon, Prince Guṇaprabha remained upon this lotus flower and, desiring to go to the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śubhārtha, prostrated himself from afar with palms joined in reverence, taking refuge three times.

At that time, the Tathāgata Kṣemārtha turned his light back to shine upon him; thereupon, the prince followed the light and went to where the Buddha was, prostrating at the Buddha’s feet and beholding the World-Honored One’s faculties in perfect tranquility.
At that time, Prince Virtue-Light (Guṇaprabha) praised the Tathāgata Auspicious Meaning (Kalyāṇārtha) with a verse, speaking in song:
"I have not long beheld the name of the King of Physicians; Now, suddenly, I am able to see the Buddha.
How is it that by establishing oneself even in defiled conduct, One is able to bring forth the attainment of all dharmas?"
Just now, at the hour of midnight, I heard from the various devas that the Buddha is without conceptualization;
having heard this, I am filled with sorrow and no longer find joy—what person could remain free from heedlessness?
To those who have lost their way, show the correct path; to those without eyes, grant equal vision.
Now I pray that you manifest the Great Way for me, and with compassionate pity, heal my ailment so that my faith may be purified.
May you cause the poor among the multitude to obtain wealth and joy; may those imprisoned in dungeons attain liberation;
may you sever our doubts and eliminate all fetters—our only wish is that you explain the practice of the Way.
Manifesting the True Dharma for me to distance me from non-Buddhists, acting as a lamp amidst the darkness,
and removing defilements for all who are harmed— I pray that the Great Physician King will sever my doubts.
May you deliver me from the path of birth and death, sever all that I hold dear,
enable me to cross over the ocean of sorrow and anxiety, and lead me through the Eightfold Path into the Mahāyāna.
Now that my lifespan is short and the life of the Dharma has ended, there are many obstacles that hinder meritorious practice;
those without merit do not have their wishes fulfilled, but now I shall open the way for their aspirations and resolve their doubts.
Now I hear the Guide’s definitive essentials: how is it that a bodhisattva may yet be heedless?
How can one practice the sublime path of the Honored Buddha and deliver sentient beings from the afflictions of birth and death?
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
"At that time, the Tathāgata Kṣemadatta, knowing the thoughts in Prince Guṇaprabha’s mind, extensively explained for him the practices of all bodhisattvas."

Upon hearing what that Buddha had taught, Prince Guṇaprabha immediately attained the gate of the inexhaustible dhāraṇī and acquired the five supernormal powers; he then leaped into the air, transformed into exquisite flowers, and scattered them over the Tathāgata Kṣemārtha.

"At that time, early on the following morning, King Aṅgati heard the sound of the palace ladies weeping within the prince’s quarters. His countenance immediately changed, and he went straight to the prince’s palace and asked, 'For what reason are you weeping?'"
The handmaidens replied, "Prince Deerga does not appear; we do not know where he is.
Upon hearing that Prince Deerga had vanished, King Arjuna immediately fell to the ground and, together with several thousand people, raised their voices in lamentation and weeping.
At that time, the deity of the city came to his house and addressed King Aṅgati, saying:
"Great King!
Do not weep or be distressed."
The Prince went eastward to visit the Tathāgata Kṣemārtha; he prostrated himself in greeting and knelt to serve him.

King Aṭṭhamaṅgala, hearing the voice of the divine messenger, set out with his retinue, ministers, the Prince’s inner palace ladies, and eighty-four billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of people toward the east to visit the Tathāgata Kṣemārtha. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha said to Rāṣṭrapāla:

"At that time, the Tathāgata Kṣemadharman, knowing King Atyantamati’s intention, immediately preached the Dharma to him as was appropriate, causing the entire assembly to attain non-retrogression from the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
Thereupon, Prince Virtue-Light addressed the Buddha Auspicious Meaning:
"I pray that the Buddha will accept my invitation to partake of pure food.
The Buddha then accepted it by remaining silent.
Prince Guṇaprabha said to his parents and all his kinsmen:
"Now, I pray that you, noble sirs, will encourage one another to adorn the city with ornaments and offer them to the Tathāgata; you should not harbor greed or feel any stinginess.
At this time, you should all act with one mind to provide encouragement and support, giving freely and without restraint."

Thereupon, Prince Virtue-Light (Guangde) and his retinue together offered their auspicious gifts to Tathāgata Auspicious Meaning (Jiyi), adorning him with necklaces, palaces, and city walls, without any lingering regret in their hearts.
Every day he prepared five hundred kinds of flavors to provide for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus;

for the sake of all the bhikṣus, he constructed chambers out of red sandalwood and the seven precious gems, with *maṇi* jewels serving as places for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), over which he erected canopies of interlaced precious jewels. To the south and north, there were rows of flowering trees, and at the edges were bathing pools in which *utpala* flowers grew.
Its borders were pure and stainless; its flowers had a hundred thousand petals, and a hundred thousand seats were arranged, with each bhikṣu provided with such equipment.
At that time, Prince Śrīprabha ensured that the bhikṣus had no anxiety regarding their clothing, nor did he allow them to harbor thoughts of others obtaining robes and garments exclusively.
"During those hundreds of millions of years, he never slept or lay down;
he did not think of what he loved, nor was he attached to his own body. He made offerings to the Buddha, his mindfulness remaining unwavering."
At that time, he had no thoughts of desire, nor was there any strife or agitation; his mind was free from malice, and he did not crave the kingdom.
He cherished nothing at all, having no craving for body or life, and being unattached to anything internal or external.
Thereupon, having heard the Dharma taught by the Buddha, they all received and upheld it, and did not inquire further of the Tathāgata.

From the beginning, they neither bathed nor washed their feet, nor did they anoint their bodies with perfumes; yet they felt no weariness or fatigue, nor did they ever sit down, except for the brief intervals required for eating and drinking.
"After the Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Kṣemārtha, he shall immediately construct a stūpa and monastery of red sandalwood and make offerings there for a hundred thousand years.
At the place where the Tathāgata is cremated, he shall make offerings with all the flowers, incenses, powdered incenses, blended perfumes, and musical performances of the entire world."

He erected nine hundred and forty million stupas, all adorned with the seven precious gems and rare treasures; he draped canopies over them, each offering five hundred jeweled parasols to the various stupas, as well as providing hundreds of thousands of musical instruments and all the flowers from Jambudvīpa and jeweled trees as offerings to the stupas.
Each lit hundreds of thousands of lamps, with the oil for each lamp costing hundreds of thousands [of coins], and scattered all manner of incense and flowers.
In this manner, they made complete offerings for a period of one billion years.

Thereupon, Prince Deerguang abandoned his home to study the Way and became a śramaṇa. Wearing the three dharma-robes, he constantly practiced alms-gathering; from the beginning, he did not involve himself in worldly affairs, nor did he sleep or lie down, having no thought at all for food or clothing.
Throughout the full span of four hundred million years, he constantly bestowed the gift of Dharma with wisdom, never conceiving of a self,
nor harboring doubts about others, much less seeking offerings.

Furthermore, there is no talk of birth and death; he preaches the Dharma for the multitude without encouraging them to be reborn in the heavens. He studies this practice to instruct all people and the members of his inner court, leading them to become śramaṇas.
The Buddha said to Rāṣṭrapāla:
"At that time, the deities of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens thought to themselves:

'Prince Guṇaprabha instructs all people and causes them all to become śramaṇas; we, too, shall now perform acts of service for the Three Jewels, so that the Three Jewels may be established and never cease.'"
After the Tathāgata Kṣemārtha has entered parinirvāṇa, his Dharma shall remain for sixty-four billion years, all of which will be protected by the bhikṣu Guṇaprabha.
"Prince Guṇaprabha made offerings to nine hundred and forty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas in this manner.
The Buddha said to Rāṣṭrapāla:
"Do you know the king Arjuna of that time?"
He replied, “I am not equal to him.
The Buddha said:
"That was none other than the Tathāgata Amitāyus.
Do you know who the Crown Prince Guṇaprabha was at that time?
He replied:
“[He] was not surpassed. “It was none other than my own person.
The city deity at that time was none other than the Tathāgata Anighabuddhi.”
The Buddha said to Rāṣṭrapāla:

"For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path—the most perfect enlightenment—should study the conduct of Prince Guṇaprabha and the teaching of tranquility; they should renounce affection and love, and practice without negligence."
"When I sought the unsurpassed, truly correct path, my diligent practice and exertion were such as this.
These people, however, lack such practice; they are greedily attached to food and clothing, and they worry incessantly without respite for the sake of receiving offerings."
Having distanced themselves from the Buddha-dharma, what they have studied is of no benefit; they defile and disorder the śramaṇas and destroy the bodhisattva-dharma.
They indulge their body, speech, and mind, recklessly fashioning their own arbitrary wishes and abandoning their fundamental practice.
They are greedy for robes, bedding, and furniture, as well as medicine for their ailments; they lack a sense of shame and remorse.

They take no pleasure in upright conduct or studying the Dharma of impermanence; they do not honor the venerable teachings, distance themselves from the Buddha’s practice, abandon the path within their own minds, and take no delight in the practice of liberation.
The Buddha said to Rāṣṭrapāla:
"For this reason, having heard this Dharma, you should awaken to it.
Abandon unwholesome friends; do not associate with those who practice what is not the Way; abandon all greedy desires."
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"One who studies the Path while craving profit and food Is one who does not delight in the ten powers of practice.
Abandoning the Buddha’s teaching of a hundred virtues, They fall into the families of others for the sake of gain and offerings."
Stubborn, depraved, and shameless, they indulge themselves and fall into various gatherings of greed;
for the sake of giving rise to worldly afflictions, they fall into perverse conduct, yet they say of themselves, "I possess virtuous conduct."
Though dwelling in seclusion, one wanders through the city; Seeking gain and offerings, one acts with unrestrained license.
Being far removed from liberation and the ground of emptiness, One should therefore abandon and depart from all states of existence.
Because of disrespect toward the Buddha and the True Dharma, they distance themselves from the merits of the Sangha;
abandoning the path of goodness, they fall into the three evil realms, thereby losing the eight hundred noble practices.

If there are those who hear this sutra being preached, Who thoroughly purify their minds and always practice with diligence— For Buddhas are difficult to encounter throughout countless billions of kalpas; Therefore, they should practice according to the Dharma.
Those who attain the Buddha’s Mahāyāna should constantly contemplate these phrases of merit;
having contemplated them, they should dwell with single-minded certainty, and shall thereby attain the unimpeded path of peace and security.
Always establish yourselves as noble sages and practice the contemplation of virtue; with thoughts of renunciation and contentment, restrain your own minds.
Do not abandon the field of goodness, lest you fall into the five realms of existence like ignorant fools.
Habituate yourself to dwelling in seclusion and always be diligent; do not disparage yourself nor hold others in contempt.
Reprimand and instruct yourself, and bring your mind to stillness; this is how I have originally followed the instructions of billions of Buddhas.
Not begrudging body or life, with a sincere and simple mind, Exerting diligence and showing reverence for the Dharma— For this reason, I constantly speak these words of instruction:
If one practices in this way, the Path will not be difficult to attain.
Those who hear this and rejoice in the Mahāyāna, yet fail to practice with diligence or take pleasure in listening,
will find that the wise who delight in these words shall later cast off evil and the bonds of enmity.
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:
"If there were a bodhisattva who practiced the five perfections (pāramitās), it would not equal studying this sutra and reverently practicing in accordance with its teachings."
"The merit of those [other practices] does not equal even a hundredth part of that of one who studies this sutra.
When this sutra was being preached, thirty koṭis of devas and humans conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, and all attained the stage of non-retrogression;
seven thousand bhikṣus attained the patience of non-arising and were liberated through the exhaustion of outflows.
Thereupon, the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the name of this sutra, and how should it be practiced?
The Buddha told Rāṣṭrapāla:

"This sutra is titled 'The Purification of Vows and Practices Free from Delusion. You should study and uphold it; it is that which the true beings delight in, which resolves the bodhisattva practices, and which fully encompasses all meanings."

When the Buddha had spoken thus, Rāṣṭrapāla, the devas, the people of the world, the nāgas, the spirits, and others were all greatly rejoiced; they rose, prostrated themselves before the Buddha, and departed.
The Sūtra on Prince Guṇaprabha Spoken by the Buddha
